chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Ahmad ibn Muhammad, from Ali ibn al-Hakam, from Aban ibn Uthman, from Abdullah ibn Sulayman, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about a man who sent his dog and his hawk. He said: As for the hawk, do not eat from its prey until you come to it and perform its ritual slaughter; and as for the dog, eat from it when you have mentioned the Name of God over it, whether the dog ate from it or did not eat.

key_terms.اسْمَ اللَّه: Mentioning the Name of God (bismillah) at the moment of releasing the hunting dog, a required condition
key_terms.الصَّقْر: Hawk or falcon (bird of prey used in falconry); its catch requires ritual slaughter unless one reaches it alive
key_terms.الْكَلْب: Dog, specifically the trained hunting dog (al-kalb al-mu'allam); its catch is permissible with tasmiya
key_terms.ذَكَاة: Ritual slaughter/purification; for birds of prey, required to make prey lawful

ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic ruling on eating prey caught by a falcon versus a hunting dog according to Imam al-Sadiq?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) distinguishes between two types of hunting animals: the trained falcon/hawk and the trained dog. For the falcon, ritual slaughter (dhaka) is required if the prey is still alive when the hunter arrives, because birds of prey are not intrinsically permissible hunting animals in the same way dogs are. For the trained hunting dog, if the hunter pronounced bismillah at the moment of release, the prey is permissible whether or not the dog ate from it — a key jurisprudential distinction in Shia fiqh that reflects the Quran (5:4) permitting the catch of trained hunting animals.
